# Nanoplots

> **Warning**
>
> [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot) is still experimental.

Nanoplots are tiny plots you can use in your table. They are simple by design, mainly because there isn't a lot of space to work with. With that simplicity, however, you do get a set of very succinct data visualizations that adapt nicely to the amount of data you feed into them. The main features of nanoplots include the following:

- interactivity: you can hover over data and other elements to show values
- choice of line, bar, and box plot charting
- you can annotate plots with a reference line and/or area
- plenty of easy-to-use options for composing your plots

Nanoplots shine when you want to show trends or distributions alongside other tabular data, so the reader can correlate a visual pattern with the row's other values at a glance. They are not a replacement for full-sized charts but should instead be used when the visual is supplementary context rather than the primary message. If a chart needs its own axis labels, legend, or detailed annotations, it belongs in a standalone figure. But when a compact sparkline or bar sequence adds meaning to a row without pulling the reader out of the table, a nanoplot is the right tool.

## A simple line-based nanoplot

Let's make some simple plots with a Polars DataFrame. Here we are using lists to define data values for each cell in the `numbers` column. The [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot) method understands that these are input values for a line plot (the default type of nanoplot).

``` python
from great_tables import GT
import polars as pl

random_numbers_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "example": ["Row " + str(x) for x in range(1, 5)],
        "numbers": [
            "20 23 6 7 37 23 21 4 7 16",
            "2.3 6.8 9.2 2.42 3.5 12.1 5.3 3.6 7.2 3.74",
            "-12 -5 6 3.7 0 8 -7.4",
            "2 0 15 7 8 10 1 24 17 13 6",
        ],
    }
)

GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers")
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

This looks a lot like the familiar sparklines you might see in tables where space for plots is limited. The input values, strings of space-separated values, can be considered here as *y* values and they are evenly spaced along the imaginary *x* axis.

Hovering over (or touching) the values is something of a treat! You might notice that:

- data values are automatically formatted for you in a compact fashion
- the plot elements also display pertinent values

This sort of interactively is baked into the rendered SVG graphics that [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot) generates from your data and selection of options.

Polars lets us express 'lists-of-values-per-cell' in different ways and **Great Tables** is pretty good at understanding different column *dtypes*. So, you can alternatively create the same table as above with the following code.

``` python
random_numbers_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "example": ["Row " + str(x) for x in range(1, 5)],
        "numbers": [
            { "val": [20, 23, 6, 7, 37, 23, 21, 4, 7, 16] },
            { "val": [2.3, 6.8, 9.2, 2.42, 3.5, 12.1, 5.3, 3.6, 7.2, 3.74] },
            { "val": [-12, -5, 6, 3.7, 0, 8, -7.4] },
            { "val": [2, 0, 15, 7, 8, 10, 1, 24, 17, 13, 6] },
        ],
    }
)

GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers")
```

Both forms of the `numbers` column in the two DataFrames look the same to [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot). The key for the list of values (here, `"val"`) can be anything as long as it's repeated down the column. So the choice is yours on how you want to prepare those column values.

## The reference line and the reference area

You can insert two additional things which may be useful: a reference line and a reference area. You can define them either through literal values or via keywords (these are: `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"q1"`, `"q3"`, `"first"`, or `"last"`). Here's a reference line that corresponds to the mean data value of each nanoplot:

``` python
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", reference_line="mean")
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

This example uses a reference area that bounds the minimum value to the median value:

``` python
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", reference_area=["min", "median"])
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

As an added touch, you don't need to worry about the order of the keywords provided to `reference_area=` (which could be potentially problematic if providing a literal value and a keyword).

## Using `autoscale=` to have a common *y*-axis scale across plots

There are lots of options. Like, if you want to ensure that the scale is shared across all of the nanoplots (so you can better get a sense of overall magnitude), you can set `autoscale=` to `True`:

``` python
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", autoscale=True)
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

If you hover along or touch the left side of any of the plots above, you'll see that each *y* scale runs from `-12.0` to `37.0`. Using `autoscale=True` is very useful if you want to compare the magnitudes of values across rows in addition to their trends. It won't, however, make much sense if the overall magnitudes of values vary wildly across rows (e.g., comparing changing currency values or stock prices over time).

Keep in mind the tradeoff: `autoscale=True` sacrifices within-row detail for cross-row comparability. If some rows have values in the thousands and others in single digits, autoscaling may compress the smaller series into a nearly flat line, hiding their internal variation. In those cases, independent scales (the default) are a better choice because they let each row's nanoplot use its full vertical range to show that row's own pattern.

## Using the [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options) helper function

There are many options for customization. You can radically change the look of a collection of nanoplots with the [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options) helper function. With that function, you invoke it in the `options=` argument of [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot). You can modify the sizes and colors of different elements, decide which elements are even present, and much more! Here's an example where a line-based nanoplot retains all of its elements, but the overall appearance is greatly altered.

``` python
from great_tables import nanoplot_options

(
    GT(random_numbers_df)
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="numbers",
        options=nanoplot_options(
            data_point_radius=8,
            data_point_stroke_color="black",
            data_point_stroke_width=2,
            data_point_fill_color="white",
            data_line_type="straight",
            data_line_stroke_color="brown",
            data_line_stroke_width=2,
            data_area_fill_color="orange",
            vertical_guide_stroke_color="green",
        ),
    )
)
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

As can be seen, you have a lot of fine-grained control over the look of a nanoplot.

## Making nanoplots with bars using `plot_type="bar"`

We don't just support line plots in [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot), we also have the option to show bar plots. The only thing you need to change is the value of `plot_type=` argument to `"bar"`.

Choosing between line and bar nanoplots depends on what you want to emphasize. Line plots highlight trends and continuity over time or a sequence. And they make it easy to see whether values are rising, falling, or oscillating. Bar plots, on the other hand, emphasize individual values and make it straightforward to compare magnitudes across positions. Bar plots also handle negative values more naturally, with bars projecting downward from a zero line, giving the reader an immediate sense of sign and scale.

``` python
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", plot_type="bar")
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

An important difference between line plots and bar plots is that the bars project from a zero line. Notice that some negative values in the bar-based nanoplot appear red and radiate downward from the gray zero line.

Using `plot_type="bar"` still allows us to supply a reference line and a reference area with `reference_line=` and `reference_area=`. The `autoscale=` option works here as well. We also have a set of options just for bar plots available inside [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options). Here's an example where we use all of the aforementioned customization possibilities:

``` python
(
    GT(random_numbers_df)
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="numbers",
        plot_type="bar",
        autoscale=True,
        reference_line="min",
        reference_area=[0, "max"],
        options=nanoplot_options(
            data_bar_stroke_color="gray",
            data_bar_stroke_width=2,
            data_bar_fill_color="orange",
            data_bar_negative_stroke_color="blue",
            data_bar_negative_stroke_width=1,
            data_bar_negative_fill_color="lightblue",
            reference_line_color="pink",
            reference_area_fill_color="bisque",
            vertical_guide_stroke_color="blue",
        ),
    )
)
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

The customized bars use orange fills, gray strokes, and a pink reference line. Negative values are styled separately with blue strokes and light blue fills, making it easy to distinguish positive and negative trends at a glance.

## Horizontal bar and line plots

Single-value bar plots, running in the horizontal direction, can be made by simply invoking [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot) on a column of numeric values. These plots are meant for comparison across rows so the method automatically scales the horizontal bars to facilitate this type of display. Here's a simple example that uses `plot_type="bar"` on the `numbers` column that contains a single numeric value in every cell.

``` python
single_vals_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "example": ["Row " + str(x) for x in range(1, 5)],
        "numbers": [2.75, 0, -3.2, 8]
    }
)

GT(single_vals_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", plot_type="bar")
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

This, interestingly enough, works with the `"line"` type of nanoplot. The result is akin to a lollipop plot:

``` python
GT(single_vals_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers")
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

You get to customize the line and the data point marker with the latter display of single values, and that's a plus. Nonetheless, it is more common to see horizontal bar plots in tables and the extra customization of negative values makes that form of presentation more advantageous.

## Box plots using `plot_type="boxplot"`

When the distribution of values matters more than their order, a box plot is the better choice. With `plot_type="boxplot"`, each row's values become a horizontal box running from the first to the third quartile, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend to the most extreme values that are within 1.5 times the box's width, and any values further out are outliers. Rows with fewer than 20 values also show every value as a faint point. Hovering over (or touching) a box shows the five statistics.

``` python
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", plot_type="boxplot")
```

| example | numbers |
|----|----|
| Row 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Row 4 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

Unlike the other nanoplots, box plots always share a scale across rows, so the boxes can be compared directly. The scale is horizontal, so a reference line or area is drawn vertically. Here's an example with the [pizzaplace](../reference/data.pizzaplace.md#great_tables.data.pizzaplace) dataset, where the times of a year's worth of pizza orders are grouped by weekday. The order times are seconds after midnight, so we provide a formatter to [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options) that shows them as clock times. A reference area marks the lunch hours.

``` python
from great_tables.data import pizzaplace


def clock(seconds):
    seconds = round(seconds)
    return f"{seconds // 3600:02}:{seconds % 3600 // 60:02}"


order_times = (
    pl.from_pandas(pizzaplace)
    .with_columns(
        day=pl.col("date").str.to_date().dt.strftime("%A"),
        day_num=pl.col("date").str.to_date().dt.weekday(),
        seconds=pl.col("time").str.to_time().cast(pl.Int64) // 1_000_000_000,
    )
    .group_by("day", "day_num")
    .agg(pizzas=pl.len(), seconds=pl.col("seconds"))
    .sort("day_num")
    .drop("day_num")
)

(
    GT(order_times, rowname_col="day")
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="seconds",
        plot_type="boxplot",
        reference_area=[12 * 3600, 14 * 3600],
        options=nanoplot_options(y_val_fmt_fn=clock),
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns="pizzas")
    .cols_label(pizzas="Pizzas", seconds="Time of order")
)
```

|  | Pizzas | Time of order |
|----|----|----|
| Monday | 6,485 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Tuesday | 6,895 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Wednesday | 6,946 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Thursday | 7,478 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Friday | 8,242 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Saturday | 7,493 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Sunday | 6,035 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

The box plots show that weekend orders come in later in the day than weekday orders. In [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options), the box and whiskers take their color and width from `data_bar_stroke_color=` and `data_bar_stroke_width=`, the box's thickness grows with `data_point_radius=`, and `show_data_points=False` hides the points.

## Line plots with paired *x* and *y* values

Aside from a single stream of *y* values, we can plot pairs of *x* and *y* values. This works only for the `"line"` type of plot. We can set up a column of Polars `struct` values in a DataFrame to have this input data prepared for [fmt_nanoplot()](../reference/GT.fmt_nanoplot.md#great_tables.GT.fmt_nanoplot). Notice that the dictionary values in the enclosed list must have the `"x"` and `"y"` keys. Further to this, the list lengths for each of `"x"` and `"y"` must match (i.e., to make valid pairs of *x* and *y*).

``` python
weather_2 = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "station": ["Station " + str(x) for x in range(1, 4)],
        "temperatures": [
            {
                "x": [6.1, 8.0, 10.1, 10.5, 11.2, 12.4, 13.1, 15.3],
                "y": [24.2, 28.2, 30.2, 30.5, 30.5, 33.1, 33.5, 32.7],
            },
            {
                "x": [7.1, 8.2, 10.3, 10.75, 11.25, 12.5, 13.5, 14.2],
                "y": [18.2, 18.1, 20.3, 20.5, 21.4, 21.9, 23.1, 23.3],
            },
            {
                "x": [6.3, 7.1, 10.3, 11.0, 12.07, 13.1, 15.12, 16.42],
                "y": [15.2, 17.77, 21.42, 21.63, 25.23, 26.84, 27.2, 27.44],
            },
        ]
    }
)

(
    GT(weather_2)
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="temperatures",
        plot_type="line",
        expand_x=[5, 16],
        expand_y=[10, 40],
        options=nanoplot_options(
            show_data_area=False,
            show_data_line=False
        )
    )
)
```

    /home/runner/work/great-tables/great-tables/great_tables/_utils_nanoplots.py:2048: UserWarning: A curved data line is not supported when `x_vals` is supplied; using `data_line_type='straight'` instead.
      warnings.warn(

| station | temperatures |
|----|----|
| Station 1 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Station 2 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |
| Station 3 | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |

The options for removing the *data area* and the *data line* (though the corresponding `show_*` arguments of [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options)) make the finalized nanoplots look somewhat like scatter plots.

Nanoplots bring data visualization directly into your table cells, giving readers an immediate visual sense of trends and distributions without leaving the tabular format. Between line plots, bar charts, reference annotations, and extensive customization through [nanoplot_options()](../reference/nanoplot_options.md#great_tables.nanoplot_options), you can tailor these compact visualizations to match your data and your presentation style.
